name: CMT type 2A (MFN2, axonal)
aliases: axonal hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy

clinicalPearls: Most common axonal (type 2) CMT, usually autosomal dominant, caused by variants in MFN2, which encodes mitofusin 2, a mitochondrial outer-membrane fusion protein
Presents with distal weakness, wasting and sensory loss in a length-dependent pattern, often with earlier and more severe onset than demyelinating CMT
Nerve conduction studies show preserved or only mildly slowed conduction velocities but markedly reduced compound motor and sensory amplitudes, reflecting axonal loss
Additional features can include optic atrophy, subclinical central white-matter changes and, in some cases, vocal cord or diaphragmatic involvement
Long axons are preferentially affected because they depend most heavily on efficient mitochondrial transport and function
Diagnosis combines the axonal electrophysiological pattern with identification of a pathogenic MFN2 variant
Management is supportive with orthoses, physiotherapy, gait aids and avoidance of neurotoxic drugs
reference.pathophysiology: MFN2 encodes mitofusin 2, a GTPase in the outer mitochondrial membrane that mediates mitochondrial fusion and contributes to mitochondrial transport along axons and to mitochondrial-endoplasmic reticulum contact. Pathogenic variants impair mitochondrial dynamics and axonal transport, starving the distal ends of the longest peripheral axons of energy and disrupting calcium handling. The result is a primarily axonal, length-dependent degeneration with relative preservation of the myelin sheath, which explains why conduction velocities remain near normal while response amplitudes fall. Secondary demyelination may occasionally accompany the axonal loss.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic acquired axonal polyneuropathy (diabetic, toxic, nutritional)
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in predominantly motor presentations
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies showing low amplitudes with relatively preserved velocities
MFN2 sequencing or a hereditary neuropathy gene panel
Brain MRI where central features are suspected
Screening for acquired causes of axonal neuropathy (glucose, B12, thyroid, toxins)
Assessment of respiratory and bulbar function in severe or early-onset cases
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting a superimposed or alternative disorder such as motor neurone disease
Respiratory or vocal cord involvement causing stridor or breathlessness
Visual loss from optic atrophy requiring ophthalmological review
Severe infantile-onset disease with early loss of ambulation
reference.prognosis: Highly variable; early-onset cases can lose independent walking in childhood or adolescence, whereas milder later-onset forms progress slowly. Life expectancy is usually normal unless there is significant respiratory involvement.
pitfalls: Expecting slow conduction velocities and dismissing CMT because they are near normal in this axonal form
Missing optic atrophy or central features that point towards MFN2
Confusing severe early-onset axonal CMT with an acquired or motor neurone disorder
Overlooking treatable acquired causes of an axonal neuropathy in an affected family
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Provide supportive care with physiotherapy and occupational therapy, as no disease-modifying drug is available
Fit ankle-foot orthoses and provide walking aids, podiatry and footwear for foot drop and pes cavus
Offer orthopaedic foot surgery for disabling fixed deformity
Treat neuropathic pain symptomatically and avoid neurotoxic agents such as vincristine
Monitor for MFN2-associated complications, including optic atrophy with ophthalmological review and respiratory, diaphragmatic and vocal cord involvement in severe or early-onset disease
Assess and support respiratory function where diaphragmatic weakness is suspected
Offer genetic counselling for the usually autosomal dominant inheritance and assess at-risk relatives
Coordinate multidisciplinary neuromuscular, orthopaedic and rehabilitation care
